title: Chapter 5.5 — Solving Equations by Graphing

hints: The equation is in terms of $x$.

questions.prompt: Solve $x + 4 = -x$ by graphing. What is the $x$-value of the intersection?

confusionCorner.body: When solving $ax + b = cx + d$, the solution is [[imp:just the $x$-coordinate]] of the intersection point. The $y$-coordinate is the common value, but the equation only asks for $x$.
confusionCorner.title: Solution is x, Not the Ordered Pair

discoveryHook.scenario: When an equation has variables on both sides, you can think of it as two separate lines. Solving the equation is just finding where those two lines intersect! It's like finding the meeting point of two runners on a track.

explanation: To solve an equation of the form $ax + b = cx + d$ by graphing, write two linear equations: $y = ax + b$ and $y = cx + d$.
Graph both lines on the same coordinate plane. The $x$-coordinate of the intersection point is the solution to the original equation.
Check the solution by substituting the $x$-value back into the original equation.
If the lines are parallel, the equation has no solution. If they are the same line, the equation has infinitely many solutions.
This method works because the intersection point satisfies both equations, meaning the left and right sides are equal at that $x$-value.

notes: The $y$-coordinate of the intersection is the common output value.
Only the $x$-coordinate is the solution to the equation.
formulaCard.title: Graphical Solution of $ax + b = cx + d$
formulaCard.formula: $$ y_1 = ax + b, \quad y_2 = cx + d $$ $$ \text{Intersection point: } (x, y) \Rightarrow \text{Solution is } x $$

steps: Graph: first line has $y$-intercept 1, slope -1; second has $y$-intercept -5, slope 2.

steps: Both have slope 3 but different $y$-intercepts → parallel lines.
No intersection → no solution to the equation.

Solve $|2x| = |x+3|$ by finding the $x$-value from $2x = x+3$.

hints: Graph $x+1 = x-5$: parallel lines → no solution.

confusionCorner.body: Even though the intersections come from related equations, always check them in the [[imp:original absolute value equation]]. The graphing method for absolute value equations typically does not produce extraneous solutions because the related equations are derived correctly, but checking is good practice.
confusionCorner.title: All Solutions Must Be Checked

blocks.title: Solving Absolute Value Equations by Graphing
teacherCues: Write $|x+1| = |2x-4|$ on the board. Ask: 'What are the two related equations we get from this absolute value equation?'
Remind students: $|A| = |B|$ leads to $A = B$ or $A = -B$.

discoveryHook.scenario: Absolute value equations can split into two linear equations. By solving each one graphically—just like a regular linear equation—you can find all possible solutions. It's like checking both sides of a fork in the road!

explanation: An absolute value equation $|ax + b| = |cx + d|$ can be solved by graphing the two related linear equations: $ax + b = cx + d$ and $ax + b = -(cx + d)$.
For each related equation, write a system of two linear equations: $y = ax + b$ and the corresponding right side.
Graph each system. The $x$-coordinate of each intersection point is a solution.
Check each solution in the original absolute value equation to ensure it is not extraneous.
There can be 0, 1, or 2 solutions depending on how many intersection points exist.

notes: Each related equation is a linear equation in $x$.
Graph each as a system and find $x$-values of intersections.

steps: Equation 1: $2x = x+3$ → $x=3$. Graph $y=2x$ and $y=x+3$, intersect at $(3,6)$.

explanation: Many real-world problems compare two linear models (costs, distances, ages).
Set the two expressions equal to form an equation, then write it as a system of two linear equations.
Graph the system and find the $x$-coordinate of the intersection. This $x$-value answers the question (e.g., number of miles, years, minutes).

confusionCorner.title: Intersection Not Visible
confusionCorner.body: If you don't see the intersection, check that both equations are entered correctly and the window is large enough. You may need to zoom out (ZBox/Zoom Out) or adjust the window settings manually.

explanation: Graphing calculators can solve equations by finding intersections of graphs.
Enter the two equations as $y_1$ and $y_2$. Use the 'intersect' feature to find the point.
Adjust the window so that the intersection is visible.
For absolute value equations, enter the two sides as separate functions.
This method is especially useful when the equations involve decimals or fractions that are hard to graph by hand.

rows.1: Press Y= and enter both equations.
Set an appropriate window (xMin, xMax, etc.).
Follow prompts to select curves and guess.

notes: Make sure both graphs appear on screen.
formulaCard.title: Using a Graphing Calculator
formulaCard.formula: $$ y_1 = \text{left side}, \; y_2 = \text{right side}, \; \text{then use intersect.} $$

discoveryHook.scenario: When numbers are messy or large, a graphing calculator or online graphing tool can find intersections instantly. Technology makes solving equations by graphing fast and accurate—especially for real-world problems with decimals or big numbers.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Equations by Graphing

rows.1: Identify the equation; for absolute value, split into two.
Graph both sides as $y_1$ and $y_2$; find intersection(s).

notes: Use technology for precision with decimals.
Check all solutions, especially for absolute value equations.
formulaCard.title: Graphing Blueprint

explanation: The blueprint for solving by graphing: [[imp:Understand]] – Identify the equation to solve. Is it linear or absolute value? If absolute value, write the related equations.
[[imp:Solve]] – Write a system of two equations from each side. Graph them (by hand or with technology). Find the intersection point(s).
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the $x$-value(s) as the solution. Check in the original equation. Interpret in context if a word problem.

discoveryHook.scenario: The Understand → Solve → Conclude blueprint works perfectly for solving equations by graphing. Understand the equation, Solve by writing a system and finding the intersection, and Conclude with the answer—checked and interpreted in context.

teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework. Walk through the wedding catering problem using the blueprint.
Emphasize: 'Understand' identifies the two expressions. 'Solve' graphs them. 'Conclude' interprets the x-coordinate.

confusionCorner.body: When solving absolute value equations graphically via related equations, the intersections you find are valid because the related equations are derived correctly. However, always plug back into the original absolute value equation to be safe.
confusionCorner.title: Extraneous Solutions in Absolute Value

presenterNotes: Start with simple linear equations to build confidence. The jump from solving for x to graphing two lines is the key conceptual shift.
For absolute value equations, remind students of the two-case rule. Graphing both cases helps them see why there can be two solutions.
When using technology, walk through the exact keystrokes. Many students struggle with finding the intersect feature and setting a proper window.
The blueprint ties it all together: the same method works for any equation that can be split into two functions.
